items.content:
Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading
A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Donald Trump ’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.
The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.
But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.
The port in Qinzhou, China, on 22 October 2026. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock The new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.
The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires
The paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.
Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order. He described the strategy as building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.
By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.
China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging its overwhelming dominance over the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year, it stunned the Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.
A girl visits an installation about rare earth production at the National Museum in Beijing, China, on 24 March 2026. Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/Reuters It has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains many other restrictions . While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hit other countries for a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency has estimated that if China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.
Where does the supply chain war go from here? The Trump administration is pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.
China, on the other hand, has announced a range of high-tech export restrictions , covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.
One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.
Workers at a photovoltaic power-generation project site on 27 October 2026 in Wenling, Zhejiang province, China. Photograph: Zhou Xuejun/VCG/Getty Images China will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.
This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?
The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.

items.title: Negotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of Hormuz - The Guardian
items.summary: Negotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of Hormuz  The Guardian
items.content:
Young Iranians walk past a large anti-US wall mural in Tehran on Sunday. Iran’s foreign minister has said he hopes the US chooses ‘diplomacy over other paths’ to end the crisis. Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images
Young Iranians walk past a large anti-US wall mural in Tehran on Sunday. Iran’s foreign minister has said he hopes the US chooses ‘diplomacy over other paths’ to end the crisis. Photograph: Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images
Negotiators ‘braced for worst’ over US-Iran talks to reopen strait of Hormuz
Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Officials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday with Qatar trying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.
The United Arab Emirates envoy Anwar Gargash said another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. He said: “We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.”
He added: “Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.”
Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.
In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days.
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the country was ready for both defence and diplomacy. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose “diplomacy over other paths”. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality”. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.
Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.
Donald Trump said on Saturday the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked. He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.
Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution. Photograph: Erik S Lesser/AFP/Getty Images Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.
Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: “Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.”
Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: “Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.”

OPEC+ to Keep December Oil Output Targets Unchanged | Egypt Oil & Gas
OPEC+ to Keep December Oil Output Targets Unchanged
OPEC+ has reached an agreement in principle to keep its production targets unchanged in December at a meeting scheduled for November 1, according to Reuters.
The decision is in line with expectations that the alliance will make no further adjustments to its production policy before next year.
The online meeting will bring together seven key OPEC+ members: Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan, and Oman. It comes as Gulf producers have increased exports following months of disruption caused by the Iran war, although most are still producing significantly below their output targets.
OPEC+ comprises members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and allied producers, including Russia.
In September, the alliance completed the phase-out of a 1.65 million barrels per day (mmbbl/d) production cut, which was first agreed upon in 2023. However, disruptions caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran have reduced the production quotas of Gulf oil-producing countries.
Reuters reported in July that OPEC+ was unlikely to make further changes to its production targets during the fourth quarter of 2026, as the alliance shifts its focus to negotiations over production quotas for 2027.
Meanwhile, the group still has an additional production cut of around 2 mmbbl/d in place, involving most of its members, which is scheduled to remain effective through the end of 2026.
According to Reuters, OPEC+ would finalize its review of member countries' production capacities during the fourth quarter before setting the 2027 baseline production levels. These baselines will determine future production quotas and shape plans for gradually unwinding the remaining cuts.

items.title: Two oil tankers explode after hitting mine in Hormuz Strait, IRGC spokesperson says - The Jerusalem Post
items.summary: Two oil tankers explode after hitting mine in Hormuz Strait, IRGC spokesperson says  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
Two oil tankers explode after hitting mine in Hormuz Strait, IRGC spokesperson says
"One of the vessels is a supertanker; it is currently engulfed in flames following a powerful explosion," the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy spokesperson said.
Vessels at the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, October 2, 2026.
Two oil tankers exploded after hitting Iranian mines while transiting the Strait of Hormuz , the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy spokesperson announced in a statement to the state media channel Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting on Sunday.
The tankers "were in violation of regulations," the spokesperson said, explaining that they were traveling on "an unauthorized route in the Strait."
"One of the vessels is a supertanker; it is currently engulfed in flames following a powerful explosion," the statement added.
The IRGC spokesperson added that oil tankers had switched off the navigation and identification systems, as they wanted " to pass covertly through an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz with the support of the terrorist US military."
"Following the incident, [the tanker] was brought to a halt," he added.
Gambia-flagged tanker vessel Bili is pictured anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas in southern Iran, May 2, 2026. (credit: Amirhossein KHORGOOEI / ISNA / AFP via Getty Images)
An oil tanker passing through the Strait of Hormuz was hit by an unknown projectile earlier on Sunday, the United Kingdom Maritime and Trade Operations (UKMTO) Center announced.
The master of a nearby tanker reported that the other vessel had been struck, UKMTO explained.
The incidents come amid repeated attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important oil export routes, since the outbreak of the conflict between the US and Iran in February.
Iran has hit vessels it says have violated its restrictions on passage through the strategic waterway, as it seeks to assert control over the strait and exert pressure on Washington.
On Friday, the IRGC Navy spokesperson said that two oil tankers that switched off their navigation systems were involved in an incident and stopped in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz, after ignoring radio warnings and attempting to use what it described as an unauthorized route through the strategic waterway.
Iran also said on Friday that it destroyed a US unmanned vessel in the eastern Strait of Hormuz. There was no immediate confirmation from the US military.
IRGC also claimed responsibility for both Friday tanker attacks
"Early this morning, an enemy vessel operating within the operational zone east of the Strait of Hormuz was struck and destroyed by the brave personnel of the Army Navy," a spokesperson for the IRGC's Navy said in a statement.
"Furthermore, two enemy oil tankers - which had violated regulations by disabling their tracking systems and navigating through prohibited and unsafe waters east of the Strait of Hormuz, despite receiving warnings - sustained damage and caught fire after striking naval mines.
"The owners of the oil tankers shall bear full responsibility for all consequences resulting from this unauthorized transit and the disregard for safety and maritime warnings," the statement added.
"We warn the enemy that any movement, infiltration, or provocative action within areas under the surveillance of the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran will be met with a decisive and proportionate response."

items.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
items.summary: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) says North Korea was responsible for the hack.
items.content:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.
The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.
Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.
In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.
It previously said withdrawals would be resumed in phases.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack.
The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services.
Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday night, US President Donald Trump said , external the US is still unsure who the culprits are.
"We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," he said.
Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.
From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.
North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.
Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".
Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners.
The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.?oc=5" target=
items.content:
Share Iran and US explore diplomacy amid rising threats of war on social media
Iran’s Foreign Minister speaks to Al Jazeera about US proposals
Tehran, Iran – Ongoing contacts through mediators have provided a potential diplomatic opening between Iran and the United States, even as both sides express readiness for renewed military escalation.
After two days of Qatari-mediated talks, Iranian authorities have signalled that a deal remains possible provided that their demands are tangibly implemented. At the same time, they have doubled down on a willingness to expand attacks or even launch preemptive strikes if they deem war is inevitable.
“We are prepared for all scenarios,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday. “We have upgraded our weaponry, addressed our vulnerabilities, and tested new arms. Our forces are at the highest level of readiness.”
His comments came as US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the talks were going “fine” but added that Iranian authorities were not “reliable”.
The Republican leader, who ordered attacks alongside Israel against Iran on February 28, has repeatedly raised prospects of once more hitting the country’s civilian infrastructure. In recent weeks, he has suggested that an attack could potentially take place after the November 3 midterm elections in the US.
“We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” Trump told reporters at a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago Club in Florida about further bombing Iran’s nuclear facilities.
The mediated talks in Tehran on Friday, and then in Qatar on Saturday, appear to have produced a new tangible result by shortening the period after which Iran’s proposal to partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz can be enforced.
Tehran had previously offered seven days, but that has now come down to two, Araghchi said in his interview with Al Jazeera.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, said there are “indications” of US interest in a negotiated settlement, citing the continuing Qatar-mediated talks and US Vice President JD Vance’s recent outreach .
“However, Iran is seeking a series of concessions while the United States insists on progress on Iran’s nuclear programme before concessions are made,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Therefore the central difficulty is sequencing and leverage. Each side wants the other to act first.”
Araghchi’s two-day offer indicates some flexibility over sequencing that could also allow both sides to claim an initial diplomatic achievement without immediately resolving their fundamental disagreements, according to Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group.
“However, the military statements show the limits of this opening. Iran appears increasingly determined to prevent a repetition of previous scenarios in which negotiations or temporary ceasefires were followed by renewed military conflict,” he wrote on social media. “From Tehran’s perspective, the objective is to make another attack so costly and unpredictable that Washington would have to reconsider the option altogether.”
As the talks were ongoing on Saturday, the office of Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said he had a meeting earlier with top military commanders to demand “maximum deterrence” through preparedness for an immediate response “without geographical restriction” to any threat.
Targets would include “tangible and intangible” US and Israeli assets, Khamenei said. Iranian authorities have previously said if Iran’s civilian infrastructure is attacked again, seabed cables and infrastructure across the region could also become targets.
After Khamenei’s statement, commanders of the general staff of the armed forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the traditional army separately expressed readiness to launch missile, drone and other attacks in case of an escalation of conflict.
State media on Sunday also aired footage of missiles and drones being taken out of massive underground storage sites and deployed during the eight months of war so far.
The authorities also signalled that they expect more potential attacks from the US and Israel, including against Iran’s power grid.
Gholamreza Jalali, commander of the National Organization for Passive Defense, said during a speech on Sunday that they have identified 14 sectors most dependent on electricity that would need support if the war restarts, without naming any.
“Adopting preventive measures in the area of passive defence for the electricity grid is a fundamental principle that all authorities must follow up in their capacities,” he said, adding that officials were considering “network islanding” practices to create different segments that would not all be simultaneously affected by potential bombing.
In and around the Strait of Hormuz, vessels continue to be attacked if they refuse to coordinate with the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, the entity set up by Iranian authorities to enforce control and sovereignty in the critical waterway.
At least four tankers were identified as being hit on Friday and Saturday, although not all attacks are reported by vessels and monitors. According to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a vessel carrying liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) was struck by three Iranian projectiles on Saturday about 40 nautical miles (74km) south of Iran’s Lavan Island, deep into the Gulf.
Transit in the strait and surrounding waterways will not return to normal unless the US takes steps towards Iran’s conditions, security chief Mohsen Rezaei told state television during an interview on Saturday night.
For the sequencing to work, he said Tehran wants the US to lift its naval blockade that has halted oil exports and the majority of Iran’s trade, which used to be facilitated through its southern ports. The US must also issue waivers for oil sanctions, unfreeze Iran’s assets abroad, stop fighting on all regional fronts, including Lebanon, and recognise a bilateral Iran-Oman arrangement for Hormuz.
Rezaei said he has yet to respond to a letter addressed to him by Vance, although he said the missive indicated a “change in tone” that he described as “positive”.
Mostafa Najafi, a Tehran-based political analyst said to be linked with Rezaei, said if the conditions are not met, the letter is likely to go unanswered and negotiations – including on Iran’s nuclear programme – will not enter a higher level.
“It is unclear how willing Washington is to accept these demands. It is clear that not recognising rights emphasised by Iran will lead to the failure of the negotiations,” he wrote on X.
The US has also doubled down on the effectiveness of its Operation Economic Outcast involving the blockade, sanctions and pressure on overland trade and aviation.
A report by the US Treasury to inform Trump’s decision-making, which was publicised by news outlet Axios, said no new oil had been loaded onto tankers at Iran’s terminals since August 25. It also showed overseas crude deliveries were down, while Iran’s year-on-year inflation neared 90 percent in September and the national currency continued to dwindle.
The report said Iran’s economy was “crippled” by the combined measures, but did not argue that it was close to collapsing.

items.summary: Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biologyAn “inspiring” University of Cambridge scientist died in the Spanish train collision on Wednesday that killed at least 69 people.Dr Marta Shahbazi, 41, an affiliate associate professor at the Cambri
items.content:
Dr Marta Shahbazi ‘was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist’, said the Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge. Photograph: MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology
Dr Marta Shahbazi ‘was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist’, said the Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge. Photograph: MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology
Tributes paid to ‘inspiring’ Cambridge scientist who died in Spain train crash
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to a conference to receive award for scientific excellence in developmental biology
An “inspiring” University of Cambridge scientist died in the Spanish train collision on Wednesday that killed at least 69 people.
Dr Marta Shahbazi , 41, an affiliate associate professor at the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute and a group leader at the city’s Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB), was travelling on one of the trains involved in the crash near Urda in Toledo province.
The LMB said the mother of two had recently won the Spanish Society of Developmental Biology’s scientific excellence prize. She had been due to be presented with the award during its conference in El Rompido, Andalucía.
In a LinkedIn post, the LMB said it was deeply saddened by her death, which was “a profound shock and a huge loss”, adding: “Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies.”
It said she was a role model who had written eloquently about balancing her family and career, describing herself as a “mother scientist”.
Dr Roser Vento-Tormo, a group leader at the Wellcome Sanger Institute outside Cambridge, wrote: “Marta Shahbazi was a beautiful person: a close collaborator, a treasured friend, and an inspiration to me both as a scientist and as a mother.
“As a scientist, we shared so many dreams. We co-supervised two students together, and I cannot describe how much joy it was to work alongside her.
“Some of our work will still be published in the coming months, and anyone who reads it will feel the passion she poured into everything she did …
“My thoughts are with her family. Anyone who knew Marta could see how deeply they were a unit, and how much they meant to her.”
The Center for Research in Molecular Medicine and Chronic Diseases (CiMUS), based in Santiago de Compostela, Spain , paid tribute to Shahbazi as “a brilliant young researcher”.
The disaster was Spain’s second high-speed rail crash this year. Both collisions occurred on the line between the central city of Madrid, Spain’s capital, and Seville, in the Andalucía region in the south of the country.
Three days of national mourning were observed from Thursday. The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described the incident as a “tragedy” and has promised an investigation .

A riot police officer in Paris is hit by a molotov cocktail during a charge against demonstrators at the end of the nationwide day of protests in France. Photograph: Sameer al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images
A riot police officer in Paris is hit by a molotov cocktail during a charge against demonstrators at the end of the nationwide day of protests in France. Photograph: Sameer al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images
Attempted murder probe after petrol bomb thrown at French riot police
Youth-led protests end with street violence in cities across France, Germany, Switzerland, Portugal and Albania
French officials have opened an investigation into the attempted murder of a police officer and Germany’s interior minister has called for harsh penalties after peaceful and mainly youth-led protests across Europe ended in violence.
In Portugal, police – some with dogs – cleared protest camps with baton charges, while security forces in Switzerland were attacked with paving stones.
Protests over the education system, deteriorating public services, declining prospects, unaffordable housing and the spiralling cost of living have shaken a number of countries this autumn.
Violence erupted in the French capital as well as Marseille, Grenoble, Bordeaux, Lyon and Toulouse on Saturday night after an estimated 320,000 demonstrators, some in Halloween costumes, took to the streets.
Protesters in Halloween costumes gather in the La Plaine square in Marseille. Officials say 320,000 people took part in protests across France. Photograph: Sener Yilmaz Aslan/Getty Images View image in fullscreen
Protesters in Halloween costumes at an unauthorised demonstration in Marseille over the high cost of living. Photograph: Coust Laurent/ABACA/Shutterstock As the rallies ended, masked and hooded rioters arrived and caused what the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as an “extraordinary” level of violence. More than 770 people were arrested.
In Paris, the prosecutor’s office said incendiary devices were thrown at a group of about 15 gendarmes and police officers and a formal investigation had been opened for “attempted murder of persons vested with public authority”.
Injuries reportedly included second-degree burns in an incident captured on mobile phone video and shared on social media and broadcast on French television.
The level of physical violence and looting was significantly lower than on 17 October, when 2,600 people were arrested and as many as 3,000 shops pillaged in one of the worst nights of urban unrest in France’s recent history.
Riot police in action in Paris. More than 770 people were arrested across France for public order offences. Photograph: Bernard Jules/ABACA/Shutterstock In Germany, looters and rioters ⁠rampaged through Frankfurt, the country’s financial hub, damaging stores and injuring more than 100 police officers.
“The rioters and looters will be identified and held accountable,” said Alexander Dobrindt, the hardline interior minister. He singled out “violent leftwing groups and troublemakers from the migrant community”, adding: “Tough penalties must follow this breach of the peace.”
Dobrindt told the tabloid newspaper Bild that deploying a heavy police presence across multiple locations had been effective. “Excesses of ​violence like those ‌in Paris were ​prevented thanks to our ​highly committed police forces,” he said.
A protester in a Batman costume salutes in front of a fire started by rioters in Frankfurt. German authorities have promised a strong response. Photograph: Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters More than 100,000 protesters marched in over 30 German cities on Saturday to demand better ⁠education and lower living costs in protests led by the “Gen Z regelt” (Gen Z will sort it) campaign.
Hooded rioters ⁠damaged 17 Frankfurt shops, looting five of them, and threw missiles including petrol bombs, according to Roman Poseck, the state interior minister for Hesse.
More than 100 of the 1,300 police officers deployed in the city were injured and 54 suspects, ‌aged from 13 to 29, were arrested. “I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: things cannot go on like this,” Poseck said.
Most of those arrested were German nationals, the minister said, adding that police estimated they had been confronted with “between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from a migrant background”.
Violence also broke out Saturday night in Cologne, where police used water cannon to disperse the crowd, and in Berlin, where protesters attacked police with bottles and fireworks. Gen Z regelt posted a statement distancing itself from all violence.
Riot police clear Lisbon’s Rossio Square of activists protesting over housing affordability. Photograph: Manuel de Almeida/EPA In Portugal , riot police removed protesters by force from Rossio Square in Lisbon at about 4.30am on Sunday after thousands of people angry at the housing crisis marched through the city on Saturday and set up camp.
The protesters want Portugal’s minority centre-right government to withdraw a ⁠bill that makes ⁠evictions easier and ends rent caps on new leases. A smaller camp in Porto was also cleared by force.
In Albania , masked protesters hurled stones and firebombs at police in the capital, Tirana, on the margins of a demonstration demanding the resignation of the prime minister, Edi Rama, over perceived corruption.
Youths threw paving stones and firebombs at police and set fire to rubbish bins at the end of a largely peaceful protest. The interior ministry said on Friday that 350 people had been hurt in the protests, including 200 police, with 269 minors arrested.
An anti-government protest in Tirana turned violent with protesters hurling stones and petrol bombs at police. Photograph: Vlasov Sulaj/NurPhoto/Shutterstock In Switzerland, hundreds of protesters gathered in Zürich and Basel on Saturday night for unauthorised demonstrations – both of which ended in violence – under the slogan: “We’ve had enough in Switzerland, too.”
In Zürich, police used water cannon, teargas and rubber bullets to disperse rioters attacking them with fireworks, bottles and stones, Swiss media reported . A police patrol car was damaged and rubbish bins and electric bikes set on fire.
In Basel, police said about 150 people gathered in the city centre at around 9pm. Shop windows were smashed, facades tagged with graffiti and bins and bikes set on fire, with incidents also reported in Geneva.

items.title: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent
items.summary: The protests in cities across Germany - including Berlin, Hamburg and Frankfurt - came on the same day hundreds of thousands also protested in France.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: Protesters clash with police and shops looted in Germany
Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.
Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.
Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.
The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.
On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.
Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.
Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.
Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".
She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."
Image caption, Police detain a demonstrator dressed as Batman in Frankfurt
Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?
On Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed.
The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.
Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing items like trainers.
Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended.
"We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard."
Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.
Image caption, People try to break through a window of a Frankfurt shop selling weapons
Similar instances took place in other German cities, following largely peaceful demonstrations.
In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.
Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was "deeply saddening that young people who wanted to peacefully demonstrate for their future were infiltrated today by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind".
A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.
In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.
The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe.
In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.
Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests across France during the demonstrations on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
Figure caption, Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across Europe
French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail and French prosecutors later launched an attempted murder probe.
Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.
French protest organisers, the Gilet Jaune, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off , but French newspaper Le Monde has reported , external that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.
Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.
In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp that had been assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.
Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.
While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.

Giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically. Photograph: Craig Brown/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News
Giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically. Photograph: Craig Brown/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News
UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme
Exclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials say
Ministers are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme.
The UK government has drawn up plans to allow students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, sources say, and is willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities to do so.
British officials insist, however, they will only make concessions on fees if the EU allows Britain entry to its proposed protectionist industrial scheme, which will impose trade restrictions on countries outside the bloc.
Rachel Reeves says UK’s future is in EU as she backs Andy Burnham on Brexit
On Sunday the former chancellor Rachel Reeves praised the prime minister , Andy Burnham, for a willingness to think boldly about the UK’s relationship with Europe – saying she believed Britain’s future was within the EU. But in her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury when Burnham took office, she said those forging a path back towards EU membership had to make compelling arguments to the public.
Ministers hope if such an agreement is reached at a Brussels summit later this month it will unlock millions of pounds’ worth of benefits for British companies looking to do business in the EU, and show that the prime minister’s attempts to forge much closer ties with the bloc are paying off.
But giving EU students cheaper access to British universities could prove controversial domestically, especially when many graduates are calling for changes to their own student loan repayment plans.
One person with knowledge of the talks said: “We are willing to give the Europeans what they want on fees, but we will have to get something significant in return. The biggest prize we are pushing for right now is access to Made in Europe, so there is a deal to be done there.”
Andy Burnham with the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, in September. Photograph: Toby Melville/AFP/Getty Images A government spokesperson said: “We are building an ambitious, close relationship with the EU that will strengthen our economy, protect British industry, and create more opportunities for young people across the UK.”
Negotiators have been thrashing out a series of deals for months to be finalised at the long-awaited summit on 20 November. Burnham wants to use it to show his commitment to much closer ties with the EU and to lay out options for how the relationship could develop in the future, including full re-entry.
In a speech at Harvard on Monday, Reeves will say the UK’s “economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe”. Praising Burnham’s “willingness to face reality head-on”, she will say it is vital the British government can “prove to the public the benefits of a closer relationship and prove to Europe that we are serious and open to compromise”.
Before the summit, agreement is understood to have largely been reached in a number of areas, including on emissions trading, agricultural products and a youth mobility scheme, with reports suggesting up to 80,000 young Europeans could be allowed to come to Britain to work, live and study. EU member states had demanded between 100,000 and 150,000, with some arguing in favour of no quota.
The two sides are also nearing agreement to allow Britain access to European biometric databases, the Guardian has learned, which could help the UK government track asylum seekers.
What makes Andy Burnham think we can rejoin the EU? | Politics Weekly
British access to the Made in Europe scheme, which is due to be finalised next year, and European demands for cheaper fees for students at British universities are the two remaining hurdles.
EU officials say they want their students to pay fees of just over £9,000 a year rather than international fees, which can rise above £60,000. The demand briefly brought negotiations to a standstill this year, with British officials saying they had been blindsided by its inclusion in talks.
The first draft of a joint statement will be presented to EU ambassadors on Wednesday with room for text to be added or deleted up to 20 November. The agreement will include fresh commitments to strengthen efforts to end the small boat crossings in the Channel, including commitments to explore the possibility of restoring the UK’s access to EU databases.
EU diplomats say top of the UK’s shopping list is access to Eurodac, an EU database that holds fingerprints of all asylum seekers from the age of six. But they also warn there will be challenges for the UK as the database was not built for law enforcement, and sharing data with a non-EU member may not be supported by all states.
Member states are pushing for firm language on fees while the UK holds out for guarantees on Made in Europe. France dropped its opposition to the inclusion of the UK in the Industrial Accelerator Act with a proposal any country in the single market on 1 January 2020 could be involved as along as it dynamically aligned on trade measures.
Ten days ago, with talks still deadlocked, the EU discussed “decoupling” the discussion on fees from the joint statement at the summit entirely, deferring any agreement for six months . But EU diplomats still hope for an agreement to allow talks to flourish for what one called “the real reset”.
Sources have told the Guardian the government is willing to concede on fees and is prepared to pay cash-strapped universities for the income they will lose. Treasury officials have been drawing up estimates for how much such a policy will cost under various scenarios, including different levels of discounts for European students and different levels of demand for British university courses.
Two sources who have seen the costings have told the Guardian that under the most expensive scenario, which involves reducing fees to the same level as domestic students’ and very high levels of demand, the government could end up paying £450m a year. Another source said the true cost was likely to be lower, while a government official described the figure as “speculative”.
Mark Corver, an analyst of university funding and director at Campus Numerics, previously calculated it would cost the sector £140m in the first year and £400m across the three-year period of a typical course.
UK negotiators are only willing to give way on fees if they get a guarantee that British companies will be treated the same as those from the EU under the new industrial scheme.
The UK was excluded from the definition of “European” for the purposes of the scheme, prompting warnings from the British government and the UK car industry. More recently, however, France – which was the principal opponent of Britain’s inclusion in the scheme – shifted its position with a new proposal to allow British manufacturers into the system as long as the UK accepted “dynamic alignment” on EU tariffs.
This could cause a problem for the UK, which has much lower tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles than in the EU. Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, recently told the Guardian he would not set tariff policy in response to pressure from Brussels.
The UK is also working on securing access to the Schengen Information System II – a database holding records of fugitives, missing persons and stolen goods, which gives real-time alerts on their cross-border movements.
The EU commissioner responsible for migration, Magnus Brunner, had been due to meet the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, in London two weeks ago to flesh out that text, but after a last-minute cancellation, work has continued between officials at the Cabinet Office and the European Commission.

Home Iran News Now Iran Culture & Society Iran’s Retirees Protest War and Poverty as Food Prices Soar and Regime...
Iran Culture & Society Iran Economy News Iranian Regime Infighting
Iran’s Retirees Protest War and Poverty as Food Prices Soar and Regime Insiders Warn of Divisions
File photo: Fierce argument among MPs in the Iranian regime's parliament (Majlis)
Retirees protesting across Iran on November 1 openly challenged the ruling establishment's spending priorities, linking poverty and unpaid benefits to corruption, war and repression. The demonstrations coincided with a sharp government increase in wheat prices and unusually candid warnings from establishment figures that inequality, intelligence failures and political infighting are undermining regime stability.
Retirees demonstrated in Tehran, Isfahan, Ahvaz, Kermanshah, Shush, Dezful and Rasht, demanding higher pensions, affordable healthcare and payment of outstanding benefits. In Ahvaz, demonstrators reportedly chanted, “Enough warmongering, our tables are empty.” Isfahan steel retirees denounced corruption and accused officials of dishonesty, while protesters in Kermanshah and Rasht called for the release of political prisoners and an end to executions.
The protests reflected a widening political dimension to economic grievances. Pensioners challenged not only their declining living standards but also the institutions responsible for government policy, social repression and the allocation of national resources.
Iran’s regime faces mounting internal pressure: 392 illegal pension-fund directorships, depleted public finances, fuel #protests , and a worsening water crisis. Meanwhile, authorities seize a digital school’s assets, accelerate security prosecutions, and hardliners demand nuclear…
The government increased wheat prices for pasta and industrial-bread producers from 23,850 to 60,000 tomans per kilogram, a 151% increase. Producers reported that flour allocations had been disrupted before the price change was clearly communicated. The measure substantially increases production costs for basic foods at a time when households are already struggling with exceptionally high inflation.
At Tehran's Loghman Hakim Hospital, director Shahin Shadnia acknowledged severe medicine shortages and sharply rising treatment costs. He said medicines previously costing 500,000–600,000 tomans had become several times more expensive, forcing hospital staff in some cases to direct patients to outside pharmacies. Alongside sanctions and damage to pharmaceutical production facilities, domestic industry representatives have identified rising currency costs, delayed insurance payments and electricity disruptions as factors worsening the crisis.
Economist Hossein Raghfar warned that inequality and the alienation of younger generations could trigger a “social explosion.” He argued that lower-income groups, once regarded as a principal support base for the Islamic Republic, were increasingly affected by economic exclusion. Raghfar described a cycle in which authorities suppress legitimate protests, lose public confidence and respond to declining legitimacy with further violence.
Iran’s crisis deepens: Judiciary calls for #IRGC involvement in hijab enforcement, government gains sweeping fuel-pricing powers, medicines rise up to 500%, and 11 provinces face winter gas shortages. A Baluch fuel carrier reportedly dies after police gunfire. #Economic strain…
A state-television discussion featured unusually severe criticism of Iran's intelligence and security institutions. University academic Hamzeh Rahim Safavi questioned why no senior officials had been held accountable for major intelligence breaches or the billions of dollars spent in Syria.
Safavi argued that acquiring nuclear weapons would not compensate for ineffective intelligence and protection systems. State-affiliated insider Rouhollah Saeidi questioned the absence of accountability for security failures involving senior figures and sensitive facilities. Their criticism challenged the emphasis on military escalation by identifying institutional incompetence and weak oversight as central security problems.
The debate exposed disagreement within establishment circles over the causes of the regime's security failures. While hardline parliamentarians have demanded changes to nuclear doctrine and even authorization to build an atomic bomb, other establishment-affiliated voices are questioning whether the existing security apparatus can fulfill its basic responsibilities.
Iran’s domestic pressures deepen: Parliament quietly revisits sweeping #internet restrictions, food-voucher cuts threaten millions, intelligence officials announce new arrests, and transport, gas and #medicine shortages worsen. Even lawmakers warn that more controls could fuel…
An October 31, editorial defending the Supreme National Security Council accused unnamed figures of weakening the institution through irresponsible criticism. It emphasized the council's authority over defense, security and national decision-making, highlighting concern over disputes affecting one of the establishment's central coordinating bodies.
Another October 31 editorial by the IRGC-run Javan newspaper warned that factional disagreements could develop into "strategic divisions, undermine public confidence and create perceptions of political paralysis." Significantly, it acknowledged that military strength depends on public trust, economic security and social cohesion.
These warnings expose growing infighting among rival factions within the regime over its confrontational policies and calls to change Iran’s nuclear doctrine. While hardliners demand further escalation, other establishment figures question the effectiveness of its military and intelligence apparatus and warn against deepening internal divisions. The dispute reveals an establishment struggling to agree even on how to project strength and deter its adversaries, exposing the fragility of its strategic decision-making amid mounting domestic crises.
Iran’s deepening crisis: 88.7% #inflation , mass job losses, looming gas shortages, and mounting repression. Meanwhile, hardliners fear regional alliances could force a strategic retreat, erode loyalist morale, and leave the regime more vulnerable to renewed #IranProtests .
Economic Grievances Confront a Security-First Response
The day's developments reveal how economic hardship is increasingly translating into explicit political opposition. Pensioners are connecting poverty with war spending and repression, while official decisions are adding costs to essential foods and hospitals are struggling to maintain access to medicines.
At the same time, criticism from within the establishment points to failures of accountability and growing concern about factional conflict. The convergence leaves the authorities facing two closely connected problems: public dissatisfaction with deteriorating living standards and internal disputes over the institutions and policies responsible for managing the crisis. Continued reliance on coercion and military confrontation may preserve hardline positions, but it also compounds the economic and political pressures that establishment commentators themselves are warning about.

items.title: Netanyahu uses election deadlock to ramp up Iran war threats and retain power - World Socialist Web Site
items.summary: Netanyahu uses election deadlock to ramp up Iran war threats and retain power  World Socialist Web Site
items.content:
Results published on October 29 confirm that Israel’s election produced no clear winner, with neither of the two Zionist blocs having the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. The deadlock deepens Israel’s political turmoil, making it ever more likely that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will seek war as a means of perpetuating his rule.
Netanyahu’s Likud party declared victory, having won the most seats at 27, securing along with its fascistic and ultra-orthodox allies 53 seats. But while that gives him an advantage in the negotiations ahead, it does not guarantee he will form the next government. The main opposition party, led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, won 21 seats, with his “Change” bloc winning 48 seats.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu holds a device as he speaks speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters September 24, 2026 [AP Photo/Seth Wenig] It was an election campaign fought between two war criminals on how best to prosecute the genocide against the Palestinians in Gaza and extend it to the West Bank, and continue the ongoing wars against Lebanon, Syria and above all Iran.
Netanyahu has been indicted for war crimes and crimes against humanity by the UN’s International Criminal Court, while Eisenkot joined Netanyahu’s war cabinet for eight months to prosecute Israel’s war on Gaza. Eisenkot is notorious for formulating the Dahiya doctrine that calls for the use of overwhelming, disproportionate force against civilian infrastructure in enemy-controlled territory, Israel’s modus operandi in all its wars.
The election contest was a racist campaign against the Palestinians, both abroad and at home, embraced by the ultra-nationalist and “liberal” Zionists alike. It flowed inexorably from the fundamental logic of the Zionist state, founded upon the expulsion and dispossession of the Palestinians.
All the Zionist parties contesting the elections are committed to the continuation and expansion of the wars against the Palestinians. They all back US President Donald Trump’s war on Iran, pledging Israel’s services as Washington’s proxy in its bid to dominate the resource-rich region and the key transportation routes.
US President Donald Trump (right) and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hold a joint press conference announcing the US peace plan for Gaza, September 29, 2025. [Photo: The White House] Almost all the leaders of the opposition bloc, framed by the media as “moderate” or “centrist”, are former military leaders and/or politicians who have served under Netanyahu and agree with him on all essential questions, to the extent Netanyahu’s government was able to complete an almost unprecedented full four-year term.
Despite the loss of Netanyahu’s majority, support for the two blocs remained largely the same as in the 2022 election. A clear majority of voters supported ideologically right-wing parties, including Netanyahu’s bloc and at least two clearly right-wing opposition parties led by Avigdor Lieberman and Naphtali Bennett, which together hold 72 seats.
The Democrats, led by former general Yair Golan and supported by Israel’s “liberals” who support the long-dead two-state solution at some indeterminate time in the future, secured 8 seats, doubling their parliamentary strength.
It was the record 80 percent turn out by Israel’s Palestinian citizens, who constitute 20 percent of the population and traditionally boycott Israel’s elections, that changed the outcome of the election under Israel’s system of proportional representation. The two Arab parties—the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen and Ahmad Tibi and Ofir Cassir of the Hadash anti-Zionist Arab-Jewish leftist party, and the United Arab List (Ra’am), the conservative Islamic movement led by Mansour Abbas that joined short-lived 2021-2 “government of change”—secured 11 and 8 seats respectively, the highest for Arab parties in the Knesset, denying Netanyahu’s bloc a majority.
This record turnout reflected the fear and anger among Israel’s Palestinians over Religious Zionism leader and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s incitement of settler violence, with his racist calls for “Judaizing” the Galilee and the Naqab (Negev), areas of Israel where hundreds of thousands of Palestinians live. Also of concern is the decades-long institutional neglect that has led to organised crime and gang violence, including unprecedented numbers of homicides, that has escalated sharply on Jewish Power leader and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s watch.
Neither of the Arab parties offer any progressive way forward, effectively signing up to the Zionist state’s agenda and testifying to the utter collapse of the Palestinian nationalist perspective. Ra’am leader Abbas said his party wanted to be part of the next government, while Joint List chairman Jabareen said his party was prepared to help pave the way for Netanyahu’s removal from power from outside.
With the opposition to Netanyahu—Eisenkot’s Change bloc and the Arab parties—together holding 67 seats, Eisenkot has demanded the president should call on him to form a government. But a majority government would be dependent upon Eisenkot and his allies’ forming a coalition with the Arab parties. While Democrats leader Golan has called for such a coalition, Eisenkot, Bennett and Lieberman have rejected it, declaring their intention of relying only on “Zionist” parties to form the new government.
On Saturday, several thousand demonstrated in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Haifa and northern Israel to urge the Israeli opposition to make a deal with Arab parties to remove Netanyahu’s government. The Tel Aviv rally was met with a counterdemonstration by Netanyahu’s young, far-right supporters.
Netanyahu and his fascistic allies have intensified their campaign of delegitimising such an alliance. He has accused the Arab parties of “stealing” the election, supposedly with funding from Qatar, without evidence, and claimed that any government dependent upon them would “endanger Israel”. Ben-Gvir has called for the arrest of Arab party leaders and Smotrich for them to be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation. The Central Elections Committee and the police have rejected the claim that Arab parties “stole” the election.
Their campaign seems likely to succeed: the possibility of the opposition leaders going back on their word and cooperating with the Arab parties to depose Netanyahu appears to be waning. Without the cooperation of Arab lawmakers, Eisenkot would be unable to form a government, leaving Netanyahu a route to power without a majority.
President Isaac Herzog must now consult the parliamentary factions and choose the party leader with the most realistic chance of building a coalition. Netanyahu may now try to cajole opposition lawmakers into joining his coalition to build a majority, seek a national unity government or remain caretaker prime minister if negotiations fail and the country heads towards another election, which would leave him in power for another six months.
The struggle between the rival blocs will unfold under the shadow of a likely resumption of the war against Iran. Another war would serve Netanyahu’s political interests: delaying the possibility of forming an alternative government, bringing Israel back to a state of emergency, pressuring political rivals to join a unity government and wiping out the opposition.
On Sunday, Golan, the Democrats leader, warned that Netanyahu could exploit a new military attack on Iran to remain in power. Writing on social media platform X, he said, “The likelihood of another round of fighting with Iran is growing”.
His remarks came after numerous Israeli and US reports and statements suggesting that Israel and Washington are preparing to launch another attack on Iran after the US midterm elections. CNN reported shortly before Israel’s election that Netanyahu was planning to attack Iran within days, but US officials asked him to hold off, indicating that a joint operation was imminent. According to an Israeli source, IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir’s warning that an attack could disrupt the elections helped persuade the Trump administration to wait.
The actions being prepared include reinforcement of American forces in the region and warnings sent to Gulf allies that they should prepare for an intense military campaign. The Pentagon has dispatched additional air defences, ammunition and supplies and relocated personnel from vulnerable bases. An additional Patriot battery is being moved to Israel amid concerns about interceptor shortages.
Bomber and fighter preparations, reductions in diplomatic staffing and the withdrawal of exposed personnel all point to preparations for American attacks and Iranian retaliation. Iran has said it would respond to any new attacks by striking at US, Gulf and Israeli infrastructure targets in neighbouring countries.
According to the Wall Street Journal , Trump and Netanyahu spoke on Saturday morning over the phone as the US set out its plans to resume strikes on Iran. On Sunday, Trump told reporters in Palm Beach, “We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes… You probably could look at Pickaxe Mountain, and you have to take care of that.” Pickaxe Mountain is believed to be a site used to store nuclear material that has not been struck yet by the US.

items.title: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading - The Guardian
items.summary: The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading  The Guardian
items.content:
Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading
A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Donald Trump ’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.
The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.
But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.
The port in Qinzhou, China, on 22 October 2026. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock The new arms race is different from those in the past. Rather than building weapons to blow each other up, China and the US are focusing on ensuring the resilience of the international supply chains on which they rely and figuring out how to constrain – and if push comes to shove, throttle – the supply chains essential to the economic and technological progress of their rival.
The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires
The paired strategies go back at least to the Covid pandemic, when China’s Xi Jinping called on the nation to “tighten international production chains’ dependence on China, forming a powerful countermeasure and deterrent capability against foreigners who would artificially cut off supply [to China]”.
Early in the Biden administration, national security adviser Jake Sullivan articulated the American goals: to limit China’s access to a narrow set of advanced technologies with military applications without upending the global economic order. He described the strategy as building a “small yard” of forbidden tech surrounded by a “high fence” of trade and investment controls.
By now, the conflict has breached the bounds of these initial rationales. Restrictions on American tech exports, investments and technology transfers to China have proliferated over the last half decade. And they are hitting not only China’s military capabilities but slowing its technological progress writ large. And Trump’s wanton deployment of tariffs is not helping.
China, on the other hand, is becoming increasingly assertive, leveraging its overwhelming dominance over the supply of critical minerals that are essential to high-tech industries for civilian and military uses. Last year, it stunned the Trump administration by throttling exports of rare earths and magnets made from them to retaliate against US tariffs and efforts to restrict China’s access to high-end semiconductors and the lithography machines needed to make them.
A girl visits an installation about rare earth production at the National Museum in Beijing, China, on 24 March 2026. Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/Reuters It has relaxed some of these controls, but it maintains many other restrictions . While they have largely been imposed to retaliate against American actions, they have also been used to hit other countries for a variety of policies it dislikes. The stakes are high. The International Energy Agency has estimated that if China were to block the US’s and Europe’s access to rare earth magnets, it could cost their economies about $1.5tn per year.
Where does the supply chain war go from here? The Trump administration is pouring hundreds of millions into projects to mine and process rare earths and other critical minerals, hoping to close China’s lead. It is also doubling down on efforts to limit China’s access to frontier semiconductors and to bar it from buying the machinery needed to make them.
China, on the other hand, has announced a range of high-tech export restrictions , covering things such as artificial intelligence chips and solar power technology. Moreover, it has threatened to punish countries that work to reduce their dependence on its mineral inputs.
One hopes there is a path to a peaceful entente. This would probably require some shared understanding of what constitutes a legitimate national security risk that may warrant actions to block supply chains. Defining the “yard” is essential. Frustrations of standard commerce should not be dealt with on a wartime footing.
Workers at a photovoltaic power-generation project site on 27 October 2026 in Wenling, Zhejiang province, China. Photograph: Zhou Xuejun/VCG/Getty Images China will probably dominate renewable energy technologies, especially the solar power industry, into the foreseeable future. It may also dominate the electric vehicle industry. This might hurt in Brussels and Washington, but it’s not worth a war. China, on the other hand, will have to accept that its mercantilistic economic strategy is not tenable for the rest of the world. Its combination of massive export growth with zero import growth is not sustainable.
This might seem doable. And yet the odds that the world economy will remain at peace seem slim. One might recall the Axis powers’ efforts to seize territories as the League of Nations curtailed their access to raw materials in the early stages of the second world war. Or FDR’s blocking of sales of American scrap steel and oil to Japan, which likely contributed to Tokyo’s decision to attack Pearl Harbor. Today, American fighter jets, submarines and missiles use rare earth magnets. What would happen if China blocked access to these materials?
The moment is strange. It’s not that long ago that trade was proposed as perhaps the most powerful tool to deliver world peace, building positive-sum interdependence among nations. That’s over. Interdependence has become a vulnerability. As China and the United States fight over who will control the next generation of technology, trade has become a theater of war.

items.title: University of Cambridge scientist among those who died in Spanish train crash
items.summary: Marta Shahbazi was an "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist", says the laboratory where she worked.
items.content:
Image caption, Dr Marta Shahbazi, pictured in 2024, was travelling to collect a prize at an awards ceremony in her native Spain when she died
An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people.
The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.
In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".
The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.
She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.
The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself.
"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.
The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB".
Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.
Image caption, Shahbazi joined the Cambridge laboratory in 2020
Shahbazi is listed on the University of Cambridge website as a principal investigator at its Stem Cell Institute (CSCI).
Institute director Prof Bertie Gottgens said its community was "shocked and deeply saddened" by her death.
"Marta led her primary research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) alongside her roles as an affiliate principal investigator and affiliate assistant professor at the CSCI," he said.
"Across both institutes, she was highly respected for her pioneering research on early human development and valued for her collaborative spirit.
"Her creativity, passion, and generosity will be greatly missed."
The news of her death was first confirmed in a social media post , external by the CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela where Shahbazi's aunt works.
Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.

It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
