A still from a social media video appears to show the result of drone strikes on an oil refinery in Russia’s Samara oblast on Friday. Photograph: social media/Reuters
Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries
Kremlin says Kyiv is ‘simply ignoring’ US wishes days before midterm elections after reported strikes on two oil sites
Ukraine has resumed its attacks on Russian oil refineries in defiance of pressure from Donald Trump ahead of the US midterm elections, as a ceasefire in the occupied town of Oleshky ended on Sunday night.
Russian state media said on Sunday Ukrainian long-range drones had set fire to the Kstovo refinery in Nizhny Novgorod oblast overnight, soon after a major strike against another big refinery in Samara oblast, owned by the Russian state energy giant Rosneft.
The Wall Street Journal had reported that Ukraine had given in to pressure from the White House to stop bombing Russian energy infrastructure.
Ukrainian officials, however, told the Kyiv Independent newspaper that they never agreed to a demand from Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law, to pause refinery strikes for 30 days. The raids on Russia restarted on Friday, Kremlin officials said, complaining that Kyiv was now “simply ignoring” US wishes.
Trump has blamed the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , for the rise in global fuel prices, and last month lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel.
Ukraine war briefing: Oleshky truce shows de-escalation is possible, says Zelenskyy
Zelenskyy has not acknowledged the latest refinery attacks, in an apparent attempt to avoid angry US reprisals. Instead, he said his armed forces had hit a defence industry enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region that made missiles. A Pantsir missile system was destroyed, he said, as part of Ukraine’s continuing “long-range sanctions”.
A satellite image shows smoke rising from the Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery in the Samara region of Russia after a reported Ukrainian drone attack on Friday. Photograph: European Union/Copernicus/Sentinel-2/Reuters Zelenskyy said his country was obliged to retaliate because of a remorseless campaign by Moscow, using drones and ballistic missiles, against vulnerable city-based energy facilities. Four Ukrainian regions were hit by Russia overnight, with electricity cut as a result in hundreds of thousands of households.
“The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the ​deficit of ballistic missile interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said on Telegram. Kyiv experienced power cuts lasting eight to 10 hours on Sunday after a critical thermal power plant was damaged.
Zelenskyy said Russia was suffering record losses, with 54,400 military personnel killed and wounded in October – the highest monthly figure since the full-scale war began. He said Ukraine recaptured 96.2 sqkm (37 sq miles) of its territory last month, 10.4 sqkm (4 sq miles) more than Moscow managed to seize, and emphasised: “Russia is losing.”
The latest attacks came before a six-day local ceasefire brokered by the US first lady, Melania Trump, came to an end in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. Hundreds of residents were reunited with their loved ones over the weekend in northern Ukraine, with both sides hailing the evacuation mission as a success.
“The ceasefire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, has ended,” said Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, hailing what had been an “important step in our joint humanitarian efforts”.
Ukrainian observers say the Russian military used the truce to reinforce its positions and to swap hungry and exhausted troops garrisoned in Oleshky. The town sits on the left bank of the Dnipro River, to the east, and is opposite the larger city of Kherson, which Ukraine recaptured in autumn 2022. A renewed Russian onslaught is inevitable, the observers believe.
The pope said on Sunday he hoped cooperation between ⁠Russia and Ukraine in implementing the Oleshky ceasefire – the most significant since 2022 – would ⁠pave the ⁠way ​for broader peace efforts.
“I hope that the cooperation between the parties, which made this necessary humanitarian gesture possible, will strengthen their willingness to engage in dialogue,” he said during his Sunday prayer.
Trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US are likely to take place later this month, and Kremlin officials said on Sunday that Vladimir Putin was willing to talk directly to Zelenskyy by phone. They added that European leaders who support Ukraine should not be involved in any such call.
There is little prospect of a wider breakthrough, however, as the Russian president’s maximalist demands remain unchanged. He is insisting that Ukraine give up all of the eastern Donetsk oblast – which Russia has been unable to seize since 2014 – as well as further territory in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia provinces, which the Kremlin does not control but says it has “annexed”.

Shell Receives First Commercial LNG Cargo From US’ Venture Global
British energy giant Shell has received the first liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargo under a long-term sales contract from US-based Venture Global’s Plaquemines export facility in Louisiana, following the start of commercial operations at the plant’s first phase, Venture Global said on press release published on November 1.
The Malaga Knutsen LNG tanker loaded the cargo and departed on October 31, marking the start of deliveries under long-term contracts at Plaquemines Phase 1, the company added.
“Achieving commercial operations at the first phase of our second LNG project in 53 months is a testament to our team’s relentless dedication and hard work,” Venture Global’s CEO Mike Sabel said.
“We are thrilled to hit another major milestone that enables us to continue delivering reliable, affordable American LNG to the global market. We deeply appreciate the collaboration of our regulators and supply chain partners, whose shared commitment helped us deliver this project safely and on schedule,” Sabel added.
The first phase completed commissioning about 22 months after producing its first LNG. Other long-term customers expected to receive volumes include Poland’s Orlen, China’s Sinopec, CNOOC Gas & Power and France’s EDF, according to Reuters .
Contract prices are expected to be significantly below recent highs of around $34 per million British thermal units (mmbtu) at Europe’s Dutch Title Transfer Facility benchmark and $32/mmbtu at Asia’s Japan-Korea Marker, Reuters reported.
Shell is a major global LNG trader and buyer, purchasing volumes from multiple suppliers to serve customers worldwide. Its integrated gas business spans LNG production, trading, shipping and marketing.

items.title: These 3 AI Stocks Could Soon Enter the S&P 500. Are They Worth Buying Before the Move? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: These 3 AI Stocks Could Soon Enter the S&P 500. Are They Worth Buying Before the Move?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom is creating opportunities beyond tech giants. Astera Labs ( ALAB -10.93% ) , Credo Technology Group ( CRDO -8.65% ) , and Sanmina ( SANM -4.33% ) are three promising companies benefiting from rising AI spending . None of the three was added to the S&P 500 in September, and the next rebalance should take effect Dec. 21.
To be included in the S&P 500, a company requires a market capitalization of at least $22.7 billion and positive earnings. If AI spending continues to drive massive growth, these stocks could emerge as future S&P 500 candidates, potentially rewarding investors who get in early.
Astera Labs, the largest of the three by market value, comes first.
1. Connectivity chips are driving Astera Labs' rapid growth
Astera Labs develops connectivity solutions that move data between chips, memory, and other components in AI systems. As these systems become more complex, the connections between them can become a bottleneck. Astera's products are addressing that challenge. The company is already expanding beyond its established connectivity products.

Its Scorpio fabric switches help connect large numbers of AI chips, while its optical connectivity and custom solutions offer greater opportunities as AI data centers evolve.
With Astera, investors demand solid growth, as evidenced by the stock's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of almost 45 times. But the results are already showing up in earnings.
Astera has also attracted attention as a potential S&P 500 addition; in fact, its $45 billion market cap already clears S&P's $22.7 billion minimum. The main risk, however, is that its growth depends heavily on AI spending, while competition and changing connectivity standards could challenge its position.
Meanwhile, another company is tackling the broader challenge of moving data across advanced AI data centers.
2. Optical products could widen Credo's reach in AI data centers
Credo develops high-speed connectivity products spanning copper and optical solutions, helping customers move data reliably across AI infrastructure . Its portfolio includes active electrical cables, optical digital signal processors, and other networking products.
One of the most interesting developments is Credo's expansion into optical connectivity. Although copper is useful for short-distance connections, optical technology can become more attractive as data rates and transmission distances grow. This gives the company broad exposure to various networking hardware used in AI data centers.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $28.38B
Its combination of growth, profitability, and expanding product opportunities makes Credo a possible S&P 500 candidate. At $33 billion, its market value already tops S&P's $22.7 billion minimum. It was also identified among possible additions in September 2026.
That said, the company faces risks around customer concentration, competition, and reliance on AI spending. And with the stock trading at 28 times forward P/E, it could look reasonable to investors backing its AI-driven growth.
The next company offers a unique way to invest in the AI boom by manufacturing hardware that keeps data centers running.
3. Manufacturing hardware gives Sanmina a role in AI data centers
Sanmina provides manufacturing solutions for electronic and industrial systems. Its work spans areas like communications networks and cloud infrastructure. As data center operators expand their infrastructure, the demand for reliable manufacturing partners will only accelerate.
Building out data centers requires more than just chips; it involves networking equipment, power systems, and other hardware. And Sanmina's manufacturing capabilities allow it to participate in that broader supply chain.
To further strengthen its capabilities, it acquired ZT Systems' manufacturing business to expand its presence in cloud and AI infrastructure manufacturing.
Market cap Market cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary. $8.87B
Sanmina moved up from the S&P SmallCap 600 to the S&P MidCap 400 in June 2026, which provides a stronger path to potential S&P 500 inclusion. However, its $9.4 billion market value sits well below S&P's $22.7 billion minimum.
The risk is that the company earns lower margins than many chip designers, while customer concentration and slower data center spending could affect growth. But at a forward P/E ratio of just over 12, the stock could be a more value-oriented way to invest in the AI boom.
The question now is whether these three companies can sustain their growth and meet the requirements for inclusion in the S&P 500.
These AI stocks could be the S&P 500's next additions
Astera Labs, Credo Technology, and Sanmina are well-positioned to benefit from the AI spending boom, and continued growth could bring them closer to joining the S&P 500.
Investors willing to get in early may want to keep these three stocks on their radar. If these companies continue to expand, an S&P 500 inclusion announcement could be around the corner, potentially giving their shares a major boost.

How Rachel Reeves has mapped out the economic agenda for Andy Burnham’s government
On Brexit, devolution and investment, the former chancellor is eerily in tune with the man who sacked her
Which senior politician has argued that “Brexit did deep damage” and that the government seeks “not to turn back the clock but to look toward a new and stable, future relationship?”
It was not Andy Burnham, who has been the torchbearer for thinking the unthinkable on Brexit since he became prime minister. Instead, these are the words of the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, in a lecture six months ago.
Reeves has taken a more thoughtful approach on how to come to terms with life outside government than some of her fellow former ministers.
A speech at Harvard on Monday will be her first public intervention on her own record and on Britain’s future, wisely left until after John Healey’s first budget .
She will say no one in government could “be in any doubt” about her view on the damage of Brexit – and her belief that one day the UK should return to the EU fold. “Economic interests, common values and basic geographical reality all point towards Europe,” Reeves will say.
The speech, which will examine how governments can meet the public’s appetite for radicalism while maintaining credibility with financial markets, will say that pursuing a closer relationship with the EU, even rejoining, may be credible as well as radical.
“Economically, it is the credible choice. Britain’s values, and a serious assessment of the geopolitical scene today, tell us it is the radical choice too,” she will say, giving Burnham “credit for his willingness to face reality head on”.
The Treasury, where the blueprints for the Remain campaign’s “Project Fear” were drawn up, has always been the heart of pro-European sentiment in government and Reeves its biggest champion under Keir Starmer .
Her sentiment seems more aligned though with that of Burnham, who cast her out of government, than with Healey, her successor as chancellor. He has joked about his own age when asked if the UK would rejoin the EU “in his lifetime”, saying it was his job to “try and make the most of Britain’s position now”.
Within Westminster, there are more than whispers from some MPs that they have judged Reeves’s legacy and influence too harshly. Healey’s first outing at the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok saw its economists lavish praise on his predecessor, saying the UK’s deficit reduction plan “stands out” among G7 peers.
It is particularly striking how the themes of Reeves’s lecture have become the agenda for Burnham’s government. In it, she argued: “Today, what most distinguishes Britain from our closest peers is the relative underperformance of our major cities outside London, compared to their European counterparts.”
Reeves, who is the MP for Leeds West and Pudsey, said the north of England had “waited for far too long, for a government that matches warm words with concerted ambition”.
Her call to “liberate our regions from stifling Whitehall orthodoxies” sounds strikingly Burnhamesque. The main policy announced in the speech? A plan to begin giving regional leaders a share of national taxes “which have, for too long, been allocated by central government”.
That work now forms the centrepiece of Healey’s budget. If this government has its own theory of growth – Brexit and devolution – it is awkward at best that it removed the key backer of both under Starmer.
But Reeves’s main theory of growth was investment, in pursuit of which she raised employers’ national insurance.
That is the other reason for Burnham’s government to be grateful to Reeves – and for which she has received no credit. Those tax raises – despite being unpopular – gave a sense of a government willing to make hard choices while taking the risk to borrow for public investment. The fiscal rules were changed to allow for a multi-year commitment to an eventual £100bn in new capital spending.
The cash is now beginning to flow into NHS infrastructure, roads, housing, rail upgrades and energy and industrial investments. Reeves will lay out her theory in her Harvard speech this week that the shift to an investment-led growth model “required sacrifices” that a Starmer-led government failed to get the public to back.
“The challenge is to make the politics and economics, those dual tests of credibility and radicalism, line up,” Reeves will say.
She will not say – although others have – that much of the problem with Starmer’s government was the man himself, rather than the agenda.
Burnham, if he avoids an early election, may start to see some of that investment bear fruit in public and market confidence, both in upgraded public services and in Britain’s appeal as a location for private investment.
There is much that could derail all this – not least further international turmoil – but when Burnham’s government counts its success on public services, Europe, devolution and growth, Reeves will be able to claim some credit.

items.title: For JPMorgan, Amazon, fighting AI bots like Meta Muse may not be a winning long-term strategy
items.summary: As companies from Amazon to JPMorgan block AI personal agents like Meta's Muse, retail experts warn that technology that removes customer friction usually wins.
items.content:
For JPMorgan, Amazon, resisting AI bots like Meta Muse won't be easy
JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon recently said the bank will block external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers, citing security risks. Amazon, Schwab and Kohl's have made similar moves.
But research from Accenture shows that 71% of customers would welcome an AI assistant like Meta Muse embedded within their primary bank's mobile app.
"We've seen this movie before," said Michael Abbott, global banking lead at Accenture. "The institutions that win are usually the ones that find a way to participate safely rather than resist the change."
The biggest names in banking and retail are starting to fight the tech titans, and one another, over a new kind of customer: the AI personal agent.
JPMorgan Chase , Charles Schwab, Amazon , Neiman Marcus and Kohl's have moved to block personal agents like Meta Muse just as consumers start sending them out to find better savings rates , shop for deals and cancel subscriptions.
The era of agentic AI has arrived, but there is uncertainty about what the landscape will look like when virtual storefronts become flooded with AI agents or when a business tries to block them.
Reports last week of AI agents going rogue in customer accounts — and prominent politicians including Sen. Mark Warner and Sen. Bernie Sanders calling for bot legislation in response to the headlines — come on the heels of JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon saying the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on behalf of retail customers, citing security risks.
Some other retailers are leaning in. Walmart announced last week it is opening the virtual doors to AI agents that customers prefer to use. "We price products, not people, so the prices that an AI agent sees are the same prices that a human would see on Walmart.com, with applicable offers and fees shown before purchase," the company said in a blog post announcing the decision.
A recent audit of 51 large U.S. retailers' published access rules by identity-verification company Billions Network and affiliated company AmanTrue, found only 11 have taken a deliberate position on AI agents. Five, including Amazon, Kohl's and Neiman Marcus, explicitly restrict them, while 37 block shopping agents largely by accident, through older bot rules written for scrapers. None has a way for a verified agent to complete a purchase.
Based on Billions Network's analysis, blocking an agent can occur in multiple ways: blocking a specific bot from a third-party by its rules (e.g. as Chewy does with an Amazon bot), and employing more general blocks on any third-party bots attempting to access login, registration and checkout functions. Its analysis of published access rules comes with the caveat that those rules are not proof of technical enforcement.
Evin McMullen, Billions Network and AmanTrue co-founder and CEO, said at this point, "Most of the retailers in our audit have not made a decision about AI agents at all."
Michael Abbott, global banking lead at the consulting firm Accenture, thinks that businesses blocking AI agents will find it difficult to win with that approach over the long term.
"If customers explicitly authorize an AI agent to act on their behalf, that's ultimately an extension of customer choice. The more important question isn't whether institutions can block agents, but whether they can create a secure and trusted way for them to engage," Abbott said.
Abbott said that Accenture research found that 65% of consumers are open to using a GPT-like financial assistant through a Gen AI platform or digital wallet, and 71% would welcome an AI assistant embedded within their primary bank's mobile app.
"We've seen this movie before … online banking, mobile banking and digital wallets. Customers tend to gravitate toward experiences that reduce friction and save time. The institutions that win are usually the ones that find a way to participate safely rather than resist the change," Abbott said.
The real opportunity for banks is to become the trusted provider of the data, intelligence and execution that those agents rely on.
"As interactions increasingly happen beyond bank-owned channels, banks still need to be present at those critical decision moments, even if they don't own the interface," Abbott said.
When it comes to distinguishing legitimate security concerns from companies protecting profits by making it harder to move money or comparison-shop, Abbott said both things can be true at the same time.
"There are very real concerns around fraud, identity verification, liability and consumer protection. And customers expect their banks to safeguard their assets and data — those responsibilities don't disappear simply because an AI agent is involved," Abbott said, adding that at the same time, consumers have historically benefited from technologies that increase transparency and make it easier to compare options.
"Our research found that 82% want to approve every AI action and 79% want the ability to immediately pause or stop AI activity. That tells us consumers are looking for convenience, but not at the expense of control," Abbott said.
Mike Danford, owner and chief revenue officer of Adverio, which runs Amazon, Walmart and Target marketplace operations for e-commerce brands, said that some of the security fears businesses, including banks, cite are less about security and more about whose sandbox a customer plays in.
"Amazon blocked Muse and other outside agents, but its own Buy for Me feature uses Amazon's agent on other brands' sites. Amazon doesn't appear worried about the agent. It's worried about who holds the data," Danford said. "Amazon now lets shoppers set rules that auto-purchase when a price threshold is met, and that's the version of agent buying consumers seem to accept, because the shopper still approves the decision within predefined parameters," he added.
"We think it's fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate," an Amazon spokesperson said. "Agentic third-party applications such as Muse have the same obligations, and we've requested that Meta remove Amazon from the experience," the spokesperson added.
Danford says banks are similar, just with a fee instead of a wall.
"JPMorgan now charges aggregators like Plaid for pulling account data, so the toll lands on the apps a consumer uses and may trickle down in subscription fees," he said.
Plaid said at the time of the September 2025 deal that it would not impact any of its existing pricing agreements with customers. Plaid does not charge consumers , though apps and services that use Plaid determine their own customer fees and subscription prices.
Evercore ISI's Mark Mahaney: Meta has proven with Muse there's appetite for an AI agent
Michael Jabbara, head of payment ecosystem risk and control at the payments network Visa, declined to speak to any single bank's motives for blocking agentic AI, but he said the fraud risks from agents are "very real and very tangible."
Consumers can be fooled by fake agents built by fraudsters to steal their credentials and payment details, he said, and a legitimate agent can act in ways the customer never intended, like buying a sofa the shopper had only asked it to find.
Agents can also behave unpredictably: Jabbara described a user who asked his agent to book a gym slot, and when the slot was taken, the agent hacked the gym's scheduling software, deleted the existing appointment and put the user's name in its place. The concerns, he said, come down to knowing "who the agent is, who the agent is acting on behalf of," and whether it has "the appropriate permissions."
"Agents are not just exchanging data. Agents can also take an action on behalf of a user," he said.
Like other experts, Jabbara says past shifts from online to mobile shopping are instructive, but for another reason: "None of those innovations really scaled until people were able to build that foundational security layer that enabled trust for that scale to happen."
Another worry is volume. Millions of agents doing legitimate work for customers could swamp websites and customer-service systems, a phenomenon some call "agentic flooding."
Amid the sudden rise of personal agents like Muse, Wharton School AI expert Ethan Mollick posted , "We will soon see what will be, in effect, a perfectly legal distributed denial of service attack on customer service departments authorized by millions of consumers when it becomes widely known that Muse/Dot/etc can make unlimited requests for old refunds, negotiate deals, etc."
Abbott calls it a possibility, not a crisis. "I see it more as an infrastructure challenge than an existential threat," he said. "Most digital systems today were designed for human interactions. Agent-driven interactions could occur at a completely different scale and frequency. One person might have multiple agents continuously monitoring rates, researching products or evaluating alternatives."
Nevertheless, he says the answer isn't to block them. "It's to build the next generation of infrastructure that can authenticate trusted agents, verify permissions, manage identity and support machine-to-machine interactions efficiently," he said.
"Customers used to interact with their banks a couple of times a month and now with mobile it is nearly daily. AI agents are just the next evolution. The organizations that prepare for that reality will be better positioned than those that try to prevent it," he said.
While many financial sites already have defenses against overuse, to protect against the types of mechanized denial-of-service attacks that have long been possible, agents "never sleep and never lose focus," said Ed Felten, a Princeton professor emeritus of computer science who served as chief technologist at the Federal Trade Commission and deputy U.S. chief technology officer in the Obama administration. And the more agents use a site, the more the costs could rise for companies like banks.
But Felten doubts the blocking will last. "When a button is clicked in the user's browser, it will be hard for a remote site to tell whether this was done by a human hand or directed by an AI agent on the user's computer," he said. "If there is a battle over AI access, it will slow the adoption of AI agents. But in the end, agents will win out because they will be so useful to users, so that sites that are too effective in blocking agents will lose business," he added.
How long can incumbents keep 'the gates' closed?
As the market forces sites to accept their customers' agents, common expectations will emerge about what is reasonable behavior by agents, experts said.
But Joseph Chalom, CEO of SharpLink, one of the largest corporate holders of the cryptocurrency ether, and a former BlackRock executive, expects the gates to stay shut for a while.
"These large incumbents effectively control the access points and will seek to keep their gates closed to fend off this innovative threat. Disruptors have fought the same battle for access for decades across travel, telephony, and financial data consolidators," Chalom said, adding that in each case, the incumbent has cited security concerns, but in fact they also face significant business model interruption.
"For example, an AI agent working for users can easily rebook flight tickets at a lower cost, eating into the margins of airlines. And more significantly, an AI agent can move idle cash from checking and savings accounts earning little interest to a money market account earning 10x the interest rate," Chalom said, noting that these types of "switching costs" are being reduced to near zero as agents have full financial literacy and attention span.
"For this reason, I don't expect any of them to be in a hurry to lower the drawbridge," Chalom said.
In the near term, Abbott says, some institutions will welcome agents while others stay restrictive as they sort out authentication, liability and governance. Longer term, he says, the data shows that companies should expect people to hand the administrative work of financial decisions to their agents. "Defense can prevent you from losing in the short term but to win banks will need an offensive strategy," Abbott said.
Proprietary bots will need to be good enough to not only keep customers but keep them from wanting to use other agents, and that is how CEOs like Amazon's Andy Jassy are talking about it. "We believe Alexa for Shopping is going to be the primary shopping agent customers use to shop Amazon. Having a shopping assistant constantly by your side as you browse, get inspired, have questions on product detail pages, and that you can simply ask to buy something based on your prior purchases that already have your history, your shipping address, and payment info, is uniquely helpful and convenient for customers," he said during last week's latest quarterly earnings call.
Ultimately, brands are about to be tested in ways that haven't been possible before. Human customers become attached to brands for reasons beyond price: a nostalgic cereal that evokes warm fuzzy childhood memories, an airline soaked in the nostalgia of family vacations, or a bank with a favorite teller. An AI agent doesn't care about any of that.
"Brand loyalty and customer relationships are getting tested. An AI agent has no feeling about a logo or a ten-year relationship. It has a mandate and cares purely about outcomes," said Nikhil Behl, president of software at FICO, the analytics company best known for credit scores. "The levers that used to create stickiness get replaced by levers an agent can actually read, such as consistent approvals, transparent pricing, fast resolution, and terms that hold up through comparison," Behl said.

The Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) dropped 5.3% in October, recording its worst monthly performance since President Trump's tariffs rocked the index in early 2025. This time, anxiety surrounding the artificial intelligence boom was the driving force behind the drawdown.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
The Nasdaq Composite plunged in October due to concerns about AI spending
The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.3% in October as investors fretted over the latest financial results from Alphabet and Amazon , while simultaneously trying to wrap their heads around the huge sums of money that technology companies are spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Capital expenditure (capex) spending among the five largest hyperscalers exceeded $400 billion in 2025, and is now forecast to approach $900 billion in 2026, per JPMorgan Chase . That represents an upward revision from $736 billion earlier in the year. Globally, JPMorgan expects AI capex spending to surpass $5.5 trillion by 2030.
Nevertheless, JPMorgan market strategist Dubravko Lakos-Bujas believes Wall Street is too pessimistic about the situation. "The Street appears to be underwriting the AI data center monetization case: Elevated capex today should ultimately translate into higher revenue, stronger margins, and expanding cash flow."
History says the Nasdaq Composite is headed much higher over the next year
Excluding last month, the Nasdaq Composite has suffered a monthly decline of at least 5% on 14 occasions during the last decade. However, the index has typically recovered quickly. The chart below shows the Nasdaq's one-year return following those incidents.
As shown above, over the last decade, the Nasdaq Composite has returned an average of 24% during the 12-month period following monthly declines of at least 5%. In other words, history says the Nasdaq Composite will climb 24% over the next year.

Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the most recent quarter, and investors panicked about return on their invested capital with respect to AI infrastructure.
However, those quarterly reports represent a single data point in what will ultimately be a much bigger picture. Personally, I don't think the investment thesis for either company has changed. Both are likely to be major winners as the AI boom unfolds, and AI itself is likely to be the most transformative technology in human history.
Short-term volatility notwithstanding, the AI boom is still a great opportunity for patient investors to make money in the stock market. To that end, now is a good time to purchase shares of the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ).
The Invesco QQQ Trust is an index fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100, a subset of the Nasdaq Composite. Following the last 14 incidents when the Nasdaq Composite dropped at least 5% in a single month, the Nasdaq-100 returned an average of 26% over the next year. Australian Stock Market Today: ASX Futures Dip On US Tech Selloff And RBA Decision
The Morning Bull - Australian Market Morning Update Sunday, 1 Nov 2026
Australian shares are set for a softer open, with SPI futures slightly in the red as global equities sell off. The dominant force today is a sharp risk off move in US markets, reflected in weaker S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures.
E mini S&P 500 futures are lower by about 1.8%, while Nasdaq 100 contracts are down roughly 3.5%. That slide comes alongside a jump in volatility gauges, with VIX futures up more than 12%, signalling a clear swing toward capital preservation over risk taking.
When equity futures and volatility move in opposite directions like this, funding costs tend to feel heavier and investors become more cautious on future earnings assumptions. Rate sensitive parts of the Australian market often see valuations compressed first as discount rates feel higher in practice, even without an immediate policy move.
The open now hinges on whether this bout of US risk aversion stabilises or deepens into Monday. Upcoming US manufacturing data and Fed commentary could either justify the repricing of growth and risk premiums or force investors to reassess how far sentiment has swung.
Mark Cutifani, former Anglo American chief executive, is joining Northern Star Resources as a non-executive director at a time when he is warning that miners which do not focus on new technology and better planning risk becoming takeover targets. Yancoal Australia has renewed key coal sale and purchase agreements with Glencore and Anotero for 2027 to 2029, locking in annual caps of up to US$750 million for sales to Glencore and US$1.2 billion for HVO-related distributions to Anotero. RBA Interest Rate Decision Tue 3 Nov. A move from 4.6% toward the 4.85% consensus would reinforce higher borrowing costs for households and corporates. Any surprise relative to that mark would likely jolt the A$ and rate sensitive stocks.
Australia Building Permits MoM Mon 2 Nov. September permits sit against a previous reading that declined 6.1%, with consensus at 2.1%. A softer outcome than that would keep pressure on construction activity and related materials names.
Australia Balance of Trade Thu 5 Nov. The September surplus forecast at A$1b compares with A$0.495b previously. A print below expectations would imply softer export momentum and could weigh on sentiment toward resource exposed parts of the Australian market.
Westpac Banking Mon 2 Nov. Final fiscal 2026 results put attention on net interest margins and bad debt charges, since these line items shape how investors think about earnings resilience for the broader Australian major bank group.
National Australia Bank Thu 5 Nov. Full year 2026 numbers will likely be read through the lens of guidance and margin trends, given NAB's role in business lending and what that says about credit conditions for Australian corporates.

If you hold this sector, focus on Tuesday's RBA meeting. Any increase in the cash rate would further tighten budgets, so upcoming trading updates that mention softer volumes or heavier discounting become important early signals for profit pressure.

Healthcare has edged higher over the past week and month after a softer 1 year and year to date run. News such as Cyclopharm's update on growing US Technegas usage shows how offshore demand can help sentiment for Australian Healthcare stocks.

Image caption, Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi led Sunday's protest
Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi for a rally demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Organised by the opposition INDIA bloc and led by Rahul Gandhi's Congress party, the protest drew many of the alliance's most prominent leaders in a show of strength against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
Protesters waved flags and chanted "Save the vote, save the country" and "Vote thief, give up power".
It was the latest in a series of protests over electoral roll revision that the opposition says has removed eligible voters to benefit the Bharatiya Janata Party. The BJP and the Election Commission deny the allegations.
The crowds gathered at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling ground in central Delhi known for hosting major political and cultural events. Some protesters sang and danced to patriotic Bollywood songs, while others waited beneath a large canopy in the colours of the Indian flag to hear opposition leaders speak.
Gandhi and several senior opposition leaders arrived at the venue in an open jeep, travelling through crowds of cheering supporters.
The event was also attended by Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, alongside leaders of regional parties such as Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav, Mehbooba Mufti, Supriya Sule and Tejashwi Yadav.
Addressing the crowds, Rahul Gandhi said those gathered had sent a message to Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar .
"This is not the voice of a single political party or of politicians. It is the voice of India's youth, women, farmers and workers," he said.
"We will not allow democracy to be destroyed in India. We will not allow the constitution to be destroyed."
Other opposition leaders echoed Gandhi's criticism of the Election Commission. Congress president Kharge said the alliance would continue its campaign until Kumar resigned, while Banerjee pledged to keep fighting against what she described as threats to democracy.
Speaking to reporters in Delhi on Sunday, senior BJP leader and federal minister JP Nadda accused the opposition of trying to create unrest and destabilise the government under the guise of defending democracy.
He described the rally as a "calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy - in the name of democracy".
Image caption, Tens of thousands of people gathered at the Ramlila Maidan
At the centre of the dispute is an exercise known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which has resulted in more than 130 million names being removed from India's draft electoral rolls.
The Election Commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate registrations and the names of people who have died, moved away or are otherwise ineligible to vote. It says eligible voters who have been wrongly excluded can seek to have their names restored.
But opposition parties allege that the process is removing legitimate voters and could benefit the governing BJP in future elections.
The controversy deepened in September when The Indian Express newspaper reported , external that Kumar had made key decisions about the revision despite repeated objections from the two other election commissioners.
The poll panel said differences of opinion were normal in any institution and did not affect its functioning.
Sunday's rally followed weeks of protests over the voter-list revision, including demonstrations by student groups and the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).
Last month, Gandhi led tens of thousands on a march from central Delhi's Connaught Place to the Supreme Court, demanding Kumar's resignation.
The CJP also backed Sunday's rally but chose not to participate. Its founder Abhijeet Dipke said the group wanted to maintain its independence from established political parties.
Image caption, People from all age groups came for the event
The event took place under strict conditions imposed by Delhi Police. According to local media reports, organisers were required to end the gathering by 5pm, install CCTV cameras at the venue and ensure that protesters did not march beyond the designated grounds.
The restrictions came against a backdrop of tensions over the policing of demonstrations in the capital. On 10 October , several leaders of the CJP were detained during protests against Kumar, while BBC reporters witnessed police dragging demonstrators away and beating some with batons.
At Ramlila Maidan, however, the atmosphere was largely peaceful, with people of different ages and professions turning out to express their concerns about the integrity of India's elections.
"We don't even know if this is a people's mandate or a stolen mandate," Isha, a development sector professional from Delhi, told the BBC.
Deepro Guha, a lawyer from Delhi, said he was concerned about the way the revision had been carried out.
"It's important because voting is the basis of democracy. If people's names are removed without any explanation, there is a problem," he said.
Image caption, Opposition alliance held a mock impeachment of CEC Kumar on Saturday
On Saturday, opposition leaders also staged a symbolic impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing him of undermining the electoral process.
The proceedings were purely symbolic and had no legal standing. Under Indian law, the chief election commissioner can only be removed through a formal parliamentary process.
But the move was another show of unity by the INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties formed in 2023 to to take on Modi's BJP.
Modi did not directly comment on the mock impeachment, but at public rallies on Friday and Saturday he accused opposition parties of trying to create chaos and undermining the dignity of the constitution.

items.title: Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - could Talarico turn the tide?
items.summary: The state's $500m Senate race may be the most closely watched in the US midterms, and is about far more than control of Congress.
items.content:
Image caption, Democrats hope James Talarico, 37, could end a decades-long winning streak for Republicans in Texas Senate races
The race for a US Senate seat in Texas may prove crucial in determining which party controls Congress next year â a significant prize in its own right - but for both parties it represents so much more than that.
For the Democrats, their losing streak in statewide elections now stretches back more than three decades. In the second most populous state in America, liberals have been in the wilderness for a generation.
But polls suggest their candidate, 37-year-old James Talarico, may be on the verge of breaking through and turning a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988.
That would be a dream scenario for Democrats - and a potential nightmare for Republicans.
"If the Democrats do pull it off, I think it's going to cause a lot of soul searching and a lot of psychological damage to the Republican Party in Texas and nationwide," said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican campaign strategist.
These dramatic stakes help explain how this Senate race has rocketed to become the most expensive in US history, with total spending reaching more than half a billion dollars.
For Talarico, it has been a remarkable rise for a candidate who in 2025 was a relatively unknown state-level Democrat.
At the Fiesta Center in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night, the line to see the softly spoken former teacher, who studied to be a Christian minister, stretched around the building and down the wide parking lot to a busy road.
In this dusty western plains town of about 250,000, which voted overwhelmingly for President Donald Trump two years ago, a visit from a major Democratic candidate on the eve of an election was unusual.
"It's just so amazing to watch," said Aaron Gonzalez, the Democratic Party chair for Hockley County, which borders Lubbock. "This time is different."
When Talarico took the stage before an estimated 3,000 supporters â with another thousand listening on speakers outside - his pitch was a familiar one for many national Democrats this year, albeit with a Texas twist.
He railed against a conservative political establishment that he said is insensitive to the economic hardship of average Americans. He condemned the corrosive influence of big money in politics. And he promised to advance a "comprehensive anti-corruption agenda" in the Senate.
"Texans are ready for change," he said. "We are done with the extremism and the corruption. We're done with the politics of division, and we are ready for something new."
The slogan for his final two weeks of campaigning â "clear eyes, full hearts, can't lose" â is taken from Friday Night Lights, a popular early 2000s TV show about a plucky small-town Texas high school football team.
His music playlist leans heavily on twangy Texas country music. He celebrates Texas breakfast tacos, quotes legendary Texas singer-songwriter Lyle Lovett and frequently mentions that his ties to the state go back eight generations.
In the Lubbock audience, Andrew Robinson, a student from nearby Texas Tech University, liked what he heard. But the 26-year-old's optimism was tempered by an entire lifetime spent watching Democrats try, and fail, to get a toehold in the state.
"A Talarico win would mean so much," he said. "I haven't been keen on wanting to stay in Texas. And if the government were to change, it could give me a reason."
Image caption, Donald Trump won Texas in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 presidential elections
For Republicans, a Democratic win in Texas would have a very different meaning.
At roughly the same time Talarico was addressing his supporters in the Fiesta Center, Trump â alongside the Republican Party's Senate candidate Ken Paxton â was just a few miles away, in a venue twice the size.
"If you go out and vote, we're going to have a tremendous win in Texas," the president told the crowd.
Trump's visit to reliably-Republican Lubbock suggests the party is concerned about turnout even in the most conservative portions of the state. It is a worry that has been echoed by other Texas Republicans.
"Understand, we could lose Texas," Texas Senator Ted Cruz said in his podcast on Friday. "The Democrats are massively out-turning-out the Republicans."
Don Huffines, who is running for election as the state's chief financial officer, issued an even more dire warning. "Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America," he posted on X.
"When the foundation breaks, it all falls apart. When we lose Texas, we lose the USA."
For weeks now, party leaders have been warning that a liberal breakthrough in the Lone Star State could have dire consequences.
They fear a Talarico win would motivate more local Democrats to run for statewide and federal offices. Better quality candidates with more funding could lead to a snowball effect similar to the Democratic inroads seen in other southern states, such as Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia.
"I think that it's pretty clear that Republicans, especially candidates, consultants, operatives, and others who are active in the party, see that this is a real threat," said Steinhauser.
"The days of waving this off and saying that Texas would never turn blue are over."
Image caption, Republican candidate Ken Paxton has a Trump endorsement - and some past controversies in Texas politics
For the Texas Senate race to come to the point where recent polls suggest Talarico has a slim but stable lead has required a unique confluence of events and political dynamics â a "perfect storm", in the words of Steinhauser.
"Everything that could go well for the Democrats is going well," he said, "and everything that could go badly for the Republicans is going badly."
But it is also a whirlwind that, in a significant part, has been sown over the past year by Trump himself.
The national environment for Republicans is a harsh one.
Voters are frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war.
Political corruption has become an issue of growing concern. Democrats, independents and many Republicans in a recent Cook political report poll identified "greedy billionaires and corporations" and politicians seeking "personal gain" as the ones to blame.
Figure caption, What's at stake for Trump in the US midterms?
Texas-specific issues have also contributed to a hostile climate for the in-power party.
Polling and recent special elections in Texas indicate that Hispanic voters â many of whom switched to Trump to help him win the White House in 2024 â have soured on the administration's immigration enforcement policies.
Hispanics make up nearly a third of the state's population - and in more than a week of early voting in Texas, they have been casting ballots in historically large numbers.
Data centre construction, which Texas Republicans had touted as a welcome investment in the state, has drawn widespread criticism, particularly in rural areas that have traditionally been solidly conservative.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott, in his own tight re-election race, recently announced a one-year moratorium on AI construction in the state â a reflection of how quickly the issue has become a political liability.
"It's bad for Republicans," one Texas political strategist, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC. "We're asking a whole lot of the electorate at this point for us to continue to be the guys in charge."
Figure caption, Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midterms
Then there's the baggage that Paxton, who defeated longtime incumbent Senator John Cornyn in a contentious primary campaign earlier this year, brings to the race.
The 63-year-old Republican successfully painted the 74-year-old Cornyn as too old and too out-of-touch with Texas conservatives. He received a late boost, just days before his run-off election victory over Cornyn, in the form of a Trump endorsement.
"Ken Paxton has gone through a lot, in many cases, very unfairly, but he is a Fighter, and knows how to WIN," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Our Country needs Fighters, and also Loyalty to the Cause of Greatness."
The "a lot" the president referenced Paxton going through includes a 2015 federal indictment on charges of securities fraud â later dropped â and a 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives on corruption, bribery and abuse of power charges.
The Texas Senate would later acquit Paxton after Trump intervened to pressure state Republican leaders.
All of this has meant that Paxton has more than a few critics â and enemies - in Texas, including within his own party.
EXPLAINED: Why Trump's approval rating matters in the midterms
IN DEPTH: The Republicans walking a Trump tightrope
Talarico, by contrast, has proven to be an effective candidate. The state legislator defeated a well-known opponent, Dallas Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, in the Democratic primary.
Since earning the nomination, he has maintained his polling lead despite a withering onslaught of negative advertising - much of it funded by the world's richest man Elon Musk, whose SpaceX company is based in Texas.
Musk alone has funnelled more than $170m into the race . Trump's MAGA Inc. committee has chipped in $40m.
While Paxton has proven to be an ineffective fundraiser, the third-party money spent on his behalf has blanketed the airwaves in the state â spilling over into sporting events involving Texas teams that air across the nation.
They have targeted Talarico for his past comments supporting transgender people, for calling "radicalised white men" a domestic terrorism threat and for criticising the fossil fuel and beef industries â two powerful interests in the state.
Talarico has distanced himself from some of those earlier comments, arguing many were taken out of context and "missed the mark" or were "deliberately provocative" or "cringy".
Meanwhile, the Texas Democrat has proven to be a historically successful fundraiser, amassing more than $140m in donations over the course of his campaign and setting a three-month fundraising record for a Senate candidate.
The funding has allowed Talarico to hit back at Paxton, highlighting his past controversies, and defending himself from Republican attacks.
He frequently leans into his religious upbringing â as the grandson of a Southern Baptist preacher who spent time in a seminary â leavening his stump speeches with biblical references.
There is one particular passage Talarico has been partial to of late â the familiar Old Testament showdown between scrappy David and the giant Goliath.
"We are going up against our own Goliaths," he said in Lubbock. "The billionaire mega-donors, the corporate special interests, the entire Washington DC establishment. Their power is real, but so is ours."
But the power of Texas Democrats has been overestimated in the past. In 2018, Congressman Beto O'Rourke posted his own historic fundraising numbers, generated serious national attention and ultimately lost to Texas Senator Cruz by just over 2%.
Talarico's polling lead, while stable, continues to rest near the margin of error in most surveys. And last-minute Republican appeals, as well as Trump's repeated campaign visits, could spur conservatives to turn out in greater numbers on election day, erasing any Democratic early voting advantages.
Inside the tiny Democratic Party office at a Talarico rally in Amarillo on Tuesday, retired schoolteacher Terri Mills listened to the candidate's stump speech.
Despite acknowledging the decades of Democratic futility and false dawns, she said she was allowing herself to hope for a Democratic victory once again.
"I have gotten my hopes up before, you know," she said. "But I do feel that this time is a little different."
Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

Will the Fed raise interest rates this year? Divided economists weigh in
The central bank has held interest rates steady five consecutive times.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh this week struck a combative tone about inflation, but the central bank opted against deploying its most powerful weapon: An interest rate hike .
"The path to central bank heaven means delivering on our remit," Warsh told reporters in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday afternoon. "This is the right team to win the battle against high inflation."
The remarks came minutes after the central bank issued its decision to hold interest rates steady for a fifth consecutive time, though pressure for a rate hike seemed to be building within its ranks.
Chair of the Federal Reserve Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference at the William McChesney Martin Jr. Federal Reserve Board Building in Washington, July 29, 2026.
Three of the 12 members on the Fed's policymaking board voted in favor of a rate hike, marking the largest number of dissenters casting ballots in the same direction since 2016.
After the announcement, economists appeared as divided as the policymakers, underscoring the uncertain prospects for a rate hike by the end of this year.
Some analysts told ABC News they expect a rate increase as soon as the Fed's next meeting in September, pointing to risks posed by price increases as global oil shortage shows little sign of letting up.
Others cast doubt on whether the Fed will raise rates at all over the remainder of 2026, noting an apparent willingness on the part of Warsh to let the market push borrowing costs higher without a nudge from the central bank.
What interest rate hikes mean for you and the economy
"Uncertainty and volatility are a feature and not a bug," Joseph Brusuelas, global economist at RSM, said in a note to investors about Warsh's stated preference that investors respond to economic events rather than Fed policy statements.
"This has turned out to be anything but a boring and uneventful summer," Brusuelas added.
The Iran war triggered a historic oil shortage that drove up fuel costs and catapulted inflation to a three-year high in May, the same month Warsh took the helm of the central bank.
A preliminary peace agreement in June offered up some relief , but a burst of on-again, off-again fighting in recent weeks has caused crude prices to rise again.
Elevated price increases pose a challenge for central bankers eager to beat back price hikes. In theory, the Fed could raise interest rates in an effort to cool off prices, but the move risks a slowdown of hiring.
Oil prices surge after Trump vows retaliation for Iranian attack
Fortunately, hiring has proven largely resilient, despite increased costs borne by shoppers and businesses.
Odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in September stand at 63%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool , a measure of investor sentiment. Odds of a rate hike by the end of the year stand at 83%.
Christa Pike issues 1st statement after surviving botched execution
Halle Berry's ex-husband Olivier Martinez awarded primary custody of their son
2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say
"I do think we're going to see a rate hike. Maybe not at the next meeting but at some time in 2026," Rebel Cole, a professor of finance at Florida Atlantic University who formerly worked at the Federal Reserve, told ABC News. "Inflation won't come down until oil prices do. The Fed is boxed in."
Some economists, by contrast, questioned whether the Fed would raise interest rates over the remainder of the year.
The Fed holds little capacity to address inflation driven by supply shortages, such as the current oil shock, Brusuelas said. Higher interest rates would instead reduce demand as shoppers and businesses weather expensive borrowing costs. The Fed may instead expect inflation to fall once oil supply returns, Brusuelas said.
"We think that the nature of the supply shock and the Fed's tendency to look through such shocks implies that the Fed has the space to keep the policy rate on hold," Brusuelas added.
Fed holds interest rates steady as economy weathers resurgent inflation
Warsh, meanwhile, has said he wants to let investors set the cost of borrowing in the market for short- and long-term bonds, instead of taking a strong hand himself through public statements or policy prescriptions.
In a sense, that approach has worked, some economists said. The 30-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2007 on Wednesday, after the Fed issued its rate decision.
The average interest rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage, which closely tracks the 10-year Treasury yield, stands at 6.66%, its highest level in a year, Freddie Mac data on Thursday showed.
"That market-delivered tightening is why the Fed could hold," Gordon Johnson, CEO and founder of data firm GLJ Research, told ABC News in a statement. "The market did the work; Warsh banked it."
A wide gap between the benchmark rate set by central bankers, the federal funds rate, and the market for Treasuries could pose challenges for policymakers, however. Investors may seek to exploit the gap, and economic tumult could result, Gerald Epstein, a professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, told ABC News.
"Eventually, the Fed would need to raise interest rates," Epstein said.
Too much focus on wonky economic questions risks overlooking the political dynamic surrounding interest rate policy, some economists said.
President Donald Trump pressured Warsh's predecessor, Jerome Powell, in an effort to reduce interest rates. The Department of Justice opened an unprecedented criminal probe into Powell, which he viewed as part and parcel of the pressure campaign. Trump has denied any involvement in the probe, which the DOJ later dropped .
Warsh has voiced support for the independence of the Fed, but he may seek to avoid rate increases even as he vows to fight inflation, especially as the political calendar barrels toward the November midterm elections, Epstein said.
"The elephant in the room is that the hawkish tone of the Fed chair is at odds with the preference of the White House for a rate cut," Brusuelas said.

items.title: Israel’s first ambassador to Somaliland presents credentials in Hargeisa
items.summary: Israel expands ties with the breakaway territory as Somalia challenges its motives and war intensifies in Yemen.
items.content:
Share Israel’s first ambassador to Somaliland presents credentials in Hargeisa on social media
Israel’s ambassador to Somaliland, Michael Lotem, left, and Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi at the ceremony in Hargeisa last month [File: Handout/Somaliland Presidency]
Israel’s first ambassador to Somaliland has presented his credentials to the breakaway territory’s president, who formally accepted them at a ceremony in Hargeisa, where officials also laid the cornerstone for an Israeli embassy.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry announced the ceremonies on Sunday, saying they were held last week.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 UN closes Somalia mission, ending three decades of political engagement
list 2 of 3 Russia-Africa Summit: What is on the agenda, and why does it matter?
list 3 of 3 US man gets 30-year sentence for Minnesota fraud that drew Trump backlash
The move puts into practice an agreement reached on December 26, 2025, when Israel became the first United Nations member state to recognise Somaliland, It declared independence from Somalia in 1991 but remains claimed by Mogadishu.
Describing it as a “historical day,” President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, known as Cirro, said during the ceremony that it was the first time a Somaliland president had received the credentials of an ambassador from a UN member state recognising its independence.
Ambassador Michael Lotem said Israel’s recognition acknowledged what Somaliland had built over 35 years, rather than serving as a mere diplomatic formality.
Somaliland has governed itself for more than three decades, but remains without recognition from any other UN member state.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said in a statement on Sunday that the exchange of ambassadors fulfilled commitments made when relations were established.
Sa’ar visited Somaliland in January and the territory opened an embassy in West Jerusalem during Cirro’s visit to Israel in June.
At the ceremony in Hargeisa, Cirro stressed the broader importance of the relationship.
“Given our strategic position around the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, our cooperation carries important regional and international significance. Let me reaffirm that Somaliland approaches this relationship with genuine strategic commitment and a long-term perspective,” he said.
Somaliland lies across the Gulf of Aden from Yemen , near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the vital shipping passage between the Red Sea and Indian Ocean.
Fighting has intensified on the Yemeni side of the strait in recent weeks.
On October 9, United Nations envoy Hans Grundberg warned that Yemen had returned to full-scale war , with battles involving the Iran-aligned Houthi movement and forces of the internationally recognised government.
Israel has also acknowledged a security relationship that predates its diplomatic recognition.
During Cirro’s visit to Israel in June, Defence Minister Israel Katz said the two sides had cooperated on secret operations for years and wanted to expand their security ties.
Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud challenged Israel’s motives in an interview with Sky News this week, saying it was seeking access to the Red Sea rather than supporting Somaliland’s independence.
“Israel wants the Red Sea, that is the only reason,” he said.
Mohamud also alleged that Israel wants a naval base in the territory.
Somaliland officials have signalled openness to hosting an Israeli military base, but the territory’s president recently said no talks had been held.
Somalia condemned Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December as a violation of its sovereignty.
Israel’s move has also been condemned by the Arab League, African Union and Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

items.content:
iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ: SOXX) forecast: Morgan Stanley warns of further 15% decline
Morgan Stanley forecasts another 10%-15% semiconductor decline
Goldman Sachs warns about semiconductor profit margins
DBS sees opportunities in memory and networking chips
SOXX ETF price forecast for November and year-end 2026
The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ: SOXX) has entered a bear market as investors reassess semiconductor valuations, AI infrastructure spending and earnings growth.
SOXX closed at $471.51 on October 30, down 28.1% from its June record of $656. The ETF plunged 8.24% on Friday following weak Intel guidance and renewed concerns about the financing of AI investments.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ: SOXX) has fallen 28.1% from its June peak of $656 to $471.51, entering a technical bear market. The fund lost 8.24% on October 30.
Morgan Stanley expects semiconductor stocks to face another 10%-15% decline before the correction ends. Goldman Sachs warns that slowing AI investment growth could weaken chipmakers' earnings.
Beinsure's SOXX forecast identifies $400-$425 as a bearish scenario, $460-$500 as the base case and $520-$540 as a potential recovery range.
The fund's five largest holdings, AMD, Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom and Intel, account for approximately 39% of its portfolio. Their earnings expectations and capital spending outlooks have a substantial influence on SOXX performance.
The selloff reflects concerns about the gap between rising AI infrastructure costs and the revenue generated by those investments.
Amazon reported negative trailing 12-month free cash flow of $42.4 bn, while Alphabet recorded approximately $9 bn in negative quarterly free cash flow. Both companies continue investing heavily in AI infrastructure.
Negative free cash flow does not necessarily indicate declining operating profitability, but sustained investment above internally generated cash raises questions about financing costs and returns on capital.
For semiconductor suppliers, the risk is that hyperscalers eventually reduce orders to protect cash flow.
Intel added pressure after forecasting Q4 revenue of $15 bn-$16 bn, below analysts' expectations of approximately $17.1 bn. Its shares fell 28.6% on October 30, despite data center revenue growing 78% to $7.3 bn in Q3.
The results exposed a divergence between AI-related server demand and the weaker PC market.
Morgan Stanley forecasts another 10%-15% semiconductor decline
Morgan Stanley chief US equity strategist Mike Wilson expects the semiconductor correction to approach its final stages around mid-November.
Wilson identified potential downside of 10%-15% for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, with support possibly emerging near 9,500 points.
The forecast was issued before the October 30 selloff and applies to the semiconductor index rather than SOXX directly.
Morgan Stanley attributes the correction to tightening financial conditions, AI financing requirements and weaker investor positioning.
The bank also notes that semiconductor earnings depend heavily on spending commitments from a relatively small group of large technology companies. A reduction in hyperscaler capital expenditure could therefore affect multiple manufacturers simultaneously.
Despite these risks, Morgan Stanley maintains its year-end S&P 500 target of 8,000, suggesting the broader equity correction may be approaching its final phase.
Goldman Sachs warns about semiconductor profit margins
Goldman Sachs Research expects hyperscaler capital expenditure to reach $1.2 tn in 2027 and $1.4 tn in 2028.
However, the bank warns that semiconductor earnings growth has benefited from strong pricing and unusually high margins.
Memory manufacturers have achieved gross margins of approximately 80%, more than twice historical levels. Goldman Sachs expects this profitability boost to moderate as supply constraints ease.
The bank also estimates that a $250 bn change in hyperscaler capital spending during 2027 could shift S&P 500 earnings growth by approximately 6 percentage points.
This illustrates how semiconductor manufacturers' earnings have become increasingly sensitive to AI investment forecasts.
Bank of America has adopted a more cautious position on Intel, downgrading the stock from Buy to Neutral and reducing its price target from $145 to $100.
Analyst Vivek Arya expects Intel's PC shipments to decline 25%-30% quarter over quarter in Q4, with further inventory adjustments possible in the first half of 2027.
The bank also estimates that weaker PC demand could create a revenue headwind of up to $750 mn for AMD, partly offset by stronger server processor sales.
DBS sees opportunities in memory and networking chips
DBS expects the semiconductor upcycle to continue through 2027-2028 but believes future performance will depend increasingly on AI economics rather than capital expenditure growth alone.
The bank identifies high-bandwidth memory, networking semiconductors and optical connectivity as potential beneficiaries of expanding AI infrastructure.
Growing AI computing clusters require faster connections between processors and greater memory bandwidth.
However, DBS warns that falling AI inference costs could eventually reduce infrastructure spending requirements unless higher usage offsets lower prices.
The bank therefore favors selective semiconductor exposure, particularly companies benefiting from supply constraints, sustainable earnings growth and reasonable valuations.
SOXX ETF price forecast for November and year-end 2026
Based on semiconductor valuations, earnings expectations and investment bank research, Beinsure identifies three conditional scenarios.
Bearish forecast: $400-$425. Further earnings downgrades, weaker AI infrastructure investment and tighter credit conditions extend the correction.
Base forecast: $460-$500. SOXX consolidates following October's decline as investors assess updated semiconductor earnings and capital spending guidance.
Bullish forecast: $520-$540. Stronger AI infrastructure orders, improving cash flow and renewed institutional demand support a recovery.
These are Beinsure's analytical scenarios, not investment bank price targets.
BlackRock has also announced a 3-for-1 SOXX share split effective November 5, 2026.
Following the split, the October 30 closing price of $471.51 would be equivalent to approximately $157.17. The bearish forecast would correspond to roughly $133-$142, the base case to $153-$167 and the bullish range to $173-$180.
The split does not change the fund's underlying value.
AMD's earnings on November 3, subsequent semiconductor guidance and hyperscaler capital expenditure forecasts will be important for the near-term outlook.
Beinsure expects continued volatility in November, with the direction of SOXX increasingly determined by earnings revisions, financing costs and the ability of AI infrastructure customers to sustain investment.
